title: Capstone: the authentication dossier
summary: Bring together everything you found on the 'HM · 1631' portrait, weigh it, and write a verdict you can defend — with your confidence stated.

shots.title:
The verdict
is yours.
shots.subtitle: Portrait of a woman, signed 'HM · 1631'.
shots.narration: Everything you've found on the case-file portrait is in your casebook. Now weigh it as a technical report would, and reach a verdict you can defend.

shots.heading: What the case file holds
items: Imaging: cracks, varnish, signature, underdrawing, X-ray
Tree rings of the oak panel
shots.narration: You have five lines of evidence: what the imaging showed, the pigments in the original paint, the tree rings of the panel, radiocarbon in the oil, and seven links of provenance.
First rule: evidence that fits the claimed date shows only that the work could be old. It can't show who made it, or that it isn't a fake.

shots.text: An anachronism is **hard to explain away** — so check the layer.
shots.narration: A material that didn't exist yet is much stronger evidence, unless it sits in a later retouching. A single-point reading can't tell which layer an element is in, so ask where the sample came from.

shots.text: Wood dates the **panel**. Paint dates the **painting**.
shots.narration: Tree rings date the felling of the tree, not the painting. An old support under new paint is a forger's classic, from Van Meegeren to Beltracchi.
Radiocarbon in the binder can do what tree rings can't: date the paint itself. Since the bomb tests, a raised carbon-14 level points to oil from the second half of the 20th century or later.
A change of mind under the paint helps attribution — but a forger can change his mind too. Weigh it alongside everything else.
The strongest case is agreement between independent methods — the eye, the laboratory and the archive. That is how the National Gallery's 'Close Examination' exhibition worked.

shots.text: Say how **sure** you are — and what would change your mind.
shots.narration: Last, state your confidence. Courts want yes or no, but evidence usually gives degrees of probability. A good dossier says what would change its mind.

points.text: Read the layers: UV shows what lies on top of the varnish, infrared shows a carbon underdrawing, and X-rays show lead white and hidden pictures.
Date materials: a pigment's earliest date gives a terminus post quem — but only for the layer it sits in.
Date wood: dendrochronology gives a felling date, with missing sapwood estimated statistically. It dates the panel, not the paint.
Date recent organic material: bomb-peak radiocarbon can place a binder after 1950, usually in two possible ranges.
Audit provenance: gaps lower confidence; anonymous owners across 1933–45 and labels without matching records are red flags.
Judge claims: separate peer-reviewed results from company claims and disputed headlines, and ask who profits.
Report honestly: attributions are graded, and good reports state their confidence.
